reading.body:
Education AI is tracked here through policy, market intelligence, and course listings, not through specific tools or infrastructure.

The four entries point to federal guidance for schools, a market-intelligence platform covering EdTech funding and AI learning platforms, and two references to a catalog of courses and credentials. The summary identifies tutoring systems, drafting assistance, and academic integrity policy as the live questions from K-12 through university. That pattern suggests the field is being defined by rules and training pathways more than by named deployments.

For AI scaling, this data offers no direct signal about compute, buildings, or power. It does not list data centers, energy demand, or hardware. What it does show is that education's AI footprint is currently administrative and pedagogical, with procurement and credentialing as the visible pressure points. Readers should not infer infrastructure constraints from this set.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau, 30.0% of firms in Educational services (NAICS 61) answered Yes to whether they had used AI in the last two weeks, down from 35.5% in the prior period. The question was first asked in September 2023, and the Bureau notes that S means suppressed. That is a short-window usage measure, not a statement about how deeply AI is embedded in teaching or administration.

The Department of Education issued the federal guidance that anchors the compliance side, and its page carries an inventory of the Department's own AI use-cases. Those use-cases are largely administrative and drafting-oriented: CAISY for real-time insights, predictive analytics and intelligent automation, Grammarly for written communication, Otter.AI for transcription of meetings, interviews and lectures, and AWS Bedrock for building and scaling applications on foundation models. The inventory also lists summarization and outlining for projects and presentations, code snippet generation, extraction of key points and action items from public documents, generation of mock data sets for testing, conversion between related data types such as county names to FIPS codes, drafting of outreach strategies and project plans, and suggested paragraphs, workflow diagrams and qualifications for public positions. One entry describes feeding the system fabricated examples of prohibited prompt information to test filters and data loss prevention.

The regulatory posture described by the Department of Education is adherence to federal regulations on AI advancement, responsible and secure usage, and innovation, in accordance with the Executive Order Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence. The sourced points summarize the guidance as framing permissible use, risk and procurement for US education. That is the frame a school or institution is working inside, and it is a governance and procurement frame rather than a performance one.

HolonIQ tracks the education economy as a market-intelligence platform, and its material here is about sizing addressable markets, quantifying demand, forecasting scenarios at varying rates of growth, and quantifying impact with rubrics, ratings and scoring to power policy, procurement and investment decisions. It also describes mapping competitive and partnership landscapes. The sourced points say it covers EdTech funding, digital transformation and AI learning platforms across K-12, higher ed and workforce learning. The excerpts do not report education-specific AI adoption rates or spending totals, so the market picture here is a description of what the platform measures rather than a set of figures.

This site's course catalog, listed under Courses and certifications are catalogued here, reports 13 AI courses, 11 of them free, 3 with public companion code, curated by level and audience with one verified source each and re-verified daily, last verified 2026-09-29. Four are university graduate courses with public materials, Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285 and MIT's 6.S191, while the rest come from industry, DeepLearning.AI, Google, Hugging Face, fast.ai and independent researcher Andrej Karpathy. The page describes university courses as generally structured around exam-driven theory and the industry courses as code-first or hands-on, and notes that membership is editorial rather than paid placement. Costs are listed as free to audit with a certificate fee, free to audit with a paid certificate, or subscription. The page states plainly that the data does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates, or which course is most widely taken.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a few narrow conclusions. The Census Bureau figure gives a measured, two-week usage share for the sector and shows the latest period at 30.0% against 35.5% in the prior period, which is a usage reading rather than evidence of returns. The Department of Education inventory shows where federal education AI use actually sits, in transcription, drafting, summarization, code assistance and testing, which is a reasonable map of low-friction starting points. None of these sources reports measured ROI for education deployments, and HolonIQ's excerpts describe market sizing and impact scoring rather than outcomes. The guidance framing of permissible use, risk and procurement suggests the binding constraints are policy and purchasing rather than model capability.

https://www.holoniq.com/.brief: HolonIQ describes itself as a platform that supplies data and research on the global impact economy. It offers tools for sizing markets, forecasting growth, and measuring impact through rubrics and ratings. The site also claims to provide competitive intelligence, partnership mapping, and strategic guidance for digital transformation. Users can receive newsletters with trending topics about impact, technology, and finance.

https://www.ed.gov/about/ed-overview/art.brief: The Department of Education's Office of the Chief Information Officer oversees the department's use of artificial intelligence in compliance with federal regulations and an executive order on AI leadership. The department has catalogued multiple AI applications across its operations, including tools for meeting transcription, writing assistance, code generation, data analysis, and document summarization. Additional uses include generating mock datasets for testing, automating data conversions, creating job descriptions, developing outreach strategies, and testing security filters. The guidance reflects the department's approach to balancing AI innovation with responsible and secure deployment.
